🎯 Objectives
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
- Use the present simple to talk about habits, routines and facts.
- Form affirmative, negative and question sentences correctly.
- Add the -s ending to verbs in the third person singular (he, she, it).
- Talk about your own daily routine using time expressions.

🔍 Warm-up
Read these three sentences and notice the underlined verbs:
- I get up at six o'clock.
- My sister gets up at seven o'clock.
- We do not go to school on Sunday.
Question: why is it "get" for I but "gets" for my sister? This lesson gives you the answer.

I. What the present simple is for
📘 Rule (functions)
We use the present simple to talk about:
1. Habits and routines: I brush my teeth every morning.
2. General facts and truths: The sun rises in the east.
3. Timetables and schedules: The train leaves at eight.
4. Likes, dislikes and opinions: She likes tea. He hates spiders.

👀 Note
The present simple does NOT usually describe an action happening right now. For that we use another tense (present continuous). Present simple = things that are generally true, not just true at this moment.

II. How to form the present simple

📏 Form (affirmative)
Subject + base verb (+ s for he / she / it)
- I / You / We / They + work, play, study, live.
- He / She / It + works, plays, studies, lives.

✏️ Worked examples
- I play football after school.
- They live in Tunis.
- She works in a hospital.
- The dog eats twice a day.

📏 The third person -s: spelling rules
1. Most verbs: add -s. work → works, read → reads, sleep → sleeps.
2. Verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: add -es. watch → watches, go → goes, do → does, wash → washes, fix → fixes.
3. Verbs ending in consonant + y: change y to i and add -es. study → studies, carry → carries, fly → flies.
4. Verbs ending in vowel + y: just add -s. play → plays, stay → stays, buy → buys.

🛠️ Method: how to decide on the ending
Step 1 — Look at the subject. Is it he, she or it (or a singular name like Sami, the cat)?
Step 2 — If NO (I, you, we, they), keep the base verb.
Step 3 — If YES, add -s or -es following the spelling rules above.

III. Negatives and questions
📏 Form (negative)
Subject + do not / does not + base verb
- I / You / We / They + do not (don't) + verb.
- He / She / It + does not (doesn't) + verb.

✏️ Worked examples
- I do not like coffee.
- We don't watch television on school nights.
- She does not eat meat.
- He doesn't play the guitar.

⚠️ Common mistakes
- After does / doesn't, the main verb has NO -s. Wrong: She doesn't likes tea. Right: She doesn't like tea. The -s is already carried by "does".
- Do not forget the auxiliary. Wrong: I not like it. Right: I do not like it.

📏 Form (questions)
Do / Does + subject + base verb ?
- Do you speak English? Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
- Does he live here? Yes, he does. / No, he doesn't.

📏 Wh- questions
Question word + do / does + subject + base verb ?
- Where do you live?
- What time does the film start?
- Why does she study every evening?

🛠️ Method: building a question
Step 1 — Start with Do (I/you/we/they) or Does (he/she/it).
Step 2 — Add the subject.
Step 3 — Add the base verb (no -s here — "does" already shows it).
Step 4 — Add a question mark.

IV. Time expressions for routines

📘 Rule (vocabulary)
Frequency and time words tell us how often or when something happens:
- every day, every morning, every week, every Sunday.
- on Mondays, at the weekend, in the evening, at night.
- always, usually, often, sometimes, never.

📏 Position of frequency adverbs

[[FIG]]<svg viewBox="0 0 680 205" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<text x="340" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="currentColor">Frequency Adverbs Scale</text>
<rect x="60" y="55" width="112" height="20" fill="#e11d48" opacity="0.85"/>

<rect x="396" y="55" width="112" height="20" fill="#16a34a" opacity="0.55"/>
<rect x="508" y="55" width="112" height="20" fill="#16a34a" opacity="0.9"/>
<text x="116" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">never</text>
<text x="116" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0%</text>
<text x="228" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">sometimes</text>
<text x="228" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">~25%</text>
<text x="340" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">often</text>
<text x="340" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">~50%</text>
<text x="452" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">usually</text>

<text x="564" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">100%</text>
<rect x="80" y="130" width="240" height="50" rx="8" fill="none" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.5"/>
<text x="200" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">Before the main verb</text>
<text x="200" y="169" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">I always have breakfast.</text>
<rect x="360" y="130" width="240" height="50" rx="8" fill="none" stroke="#e11d48" stroke-width="1.5"/>
<text x="480" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">After "to be"</text>
<text x="480" y="169" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">She is never late.</text>
</svg>[[/FIG]]
Frequency adverbs go BEFORE the main verb but AFTER the verb "to be".
- I always have breakfast. (before "have")
- She is never late. (after "is")

✏️ Worked example: a daily routine
I get up at half past six. I have breakfast and then I walk to school. Classes start at eight. In the afternoon I do my homework. My father usually comes home at five. We have dinner together in the evening. I go to bed at ten.

👀 Note
Telling the time: 6:00 = six o'clock. 6:15 = quarter past six. 6:30 = half past six. 6:45 = quarter to seven. These are very useful for describing routines.

⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid
1. Forgetting -s with he/she/it: My brother go... → My brother goes...
2. Adding -s in negatives/questions: Does she likes...? → Does she like...?
3. Using the wrong auxiliary: He don't know → He doesn't know.
4. Wrong word order with adverbs: I go always → I always go.

⭐ Recap
- Present simple = habits, routines, facts, timetables, likes.
- Add -s / -es to the verb with he, she, it.
- Negatives: don't / doesn't + base verb.
- Questions: Do / Does + subject + base verb.
- Frequency adverbs go before the main verb, after "to be".

📘 Language bank
Verbs: get up, wake up, have breakfast, go to school, study, play, watch, do homework, have dinner, go to bed.
Time: every day, in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening, at night, at the weekend.
Frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, never.
Useful sentences: What time do you get up? / I usually get up at seven. / She never watches TV in the morning. / Do you play sport at the weekend?

📝 Practice
Exercise 1 — Put the verb in the correct present simple form.
1. My mother (cook) ______ dinner every evening.
2. We (not / watch) ______ television in the morning.
3. ______ your father (work) ______ on Saturdays?
4. The bus (leave) ______ at eight o'clock.
5. Sami and Nour (study) ______ English at school.

Exercise 2 — Correct the mistake in each sentence.
1. She go to school by bus.
2. He don't like fish.
3. Does she likes music?
4. I always am tired after football.
5. My brother watch cartoons every day.

Exercise 3 — Answer about yourself.
1. What time do you get up?
2. How do you go to school?
3. What do you do after school?
4. What is your favourite meal?

✅ Answers
Exercise 1: 1. cooks 2. do not watch (don't watch) 3. Does ... work 4. leaves 5. study.
Exercise 2: 1. She goes to school by bus. 2. He doesn't like fish. 3. Does she like music? 4. I am always tired after football. 5. My brother watches cartoons every day.

🗣️ Speaking task
Work with a partner. Ask and answer about your daily routine. Use the words: get up, have breakfast, go to school, study, play, have dinner, go to bed. Try to use "usually", "always" and "never".

👀 Extra note
Remember the two golden points of this lesson:
1. Add -s (or -es / -ies) to the verb only with he, she, it.
2. In negatives and questions, "does" already carries the -s, so the main verb stays in its base form (She doesn't play, Does she play?).
Master these two ideas and most present simple mistakes disappear.

📋 Summary
- The present simple describes habits, routines, general facts, timetables and likes/dislikes — not actions happening right now.
- Affirmative: I/you/we/they + base verb; he/she/it + verb+s (add -es or change y→ies for spelling rules).
- Negative: subject + don't/doesn't + base verb — the main verb never takes -s after does/doesn't.
- Questions: Do/Does + subject + base verb? — answered with short forms (Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.).
- Wh- questions: question word + do/does + subject + base verb (Where do you live?).
- Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) go before the main verb but after "to be".
- Typical routine expressions: every day, in the morning, in the evening, at the weekend, at night.
- Golden rule to remember: "does/doesn't" already carries the -s, so the main verb after it always stays in its base form.
